leopardcubs.title: Leopard Cubs — Small, Spotted, and Curious
leopardcubs.description: Few sights in the wild are as charming as leopard cubs at play. We found two of them tumbling on a fallen log while their mother watched from the shade of a nearby tree. They pounced on each other's tails, scrambled up the bark, and paused every so often to stare at us with enormous, curious eyes. Cubs stay hidden for their first weeks, so a sighting like this is rare. Their rosette-patterned coats, still soft and fluffy, make them look more like toys than predators, but every game is practice for the skills they will need to survive.

restingleopard.title: The Resting Leopard
restingleopard.description: Leopards spend much of the day asleep, and this one had chosen a perfect branch: broad, shaded, and high enough to be safe from lions. Draped over it with limbs dangling, it looked utterly relaxed, opening one amber eye now and then to check on us. In the late afternoon it stretched, yawned, and began to groom, a reminder of how domestic cats inherit so many of their habits from these great predators. Watching a leopard at rest is quietly mesmerising. You sense the power held in reserve, switched off, waiting for dusk.

tigerdrink.title: Tiger Drinking — A Moment of Calm
tigerdrink.description: On the banks of the Ramganga, a tiger stepped out of the grass and lowered its head to the water. For a few minutes the whole forest seemed to pause. The ripples spread outward, the reflections of sal trees trembled, and the only movement was the steady lapping of its tongue. Tigers need regular access to water, which is why rivers and pools become the best places to wait. Photographing the scene required nothing but patience and a steady hand. It was a gentle, almost tender moment from an animal usually defined by power.

tigerhunt.title: Tiger on the Hunt
tigerhunt.description: The change in a tiger's body language when it begins to hunt is unmistakable. Shoulders drop, steps slow, and the eyes lock onto a single target. At Pench, we watched one stalk through the dry grass toward a herd of chital, moving in silence and pausing whenever a deer looked up. The hunt did not end in a kill that day, as most do not, but the tension was extraordinary. Tigers succeed in only a fraction of their attempts, which is why every meal is hard-won. To witness this focus up close is to understand why the species commands such respect.

tigerwater.title: Tiger in Water — The Swimmer of the Delta
tigerwater.description: Unlike most big cats, tigers love water, and nowhere is this clearer than in the Sundarbans, where they swim tidal channels between mangrove islands. From a small boat we saw one slip into the creek and cross with powerful, easy strokes, its head just above the surface. The landscape is tough, with muddy banks, salty water and thick roots, yet the tiger moved through it as if born to it. It is one of the most challenging places on earth to see this animal, and one of the most rewarding. A true sight of resilience and adaptation.

tigerwalking.title: The Walking Bengal Tiger
tigerwalking.description: There is a particular rhythm to a tiger walking, unhurried, deliberate, each paw placed with care, and shoulders rolling beneath a coat of burnt orange and black. In the elephant grass of Kaziranga, we saw one emerge onto an open track and simply walk toward us before turning aside into the reeds. No fear, no rush, just a sense of absolute ownership of the landscape. The Bengal tiger is the most numerous of all tiger subspecies, yet every individual remains precious. Watching one stroll past is a reminder that conservation, here, is working and must continue.
